LESSON 7 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

The Security Mindset

Four habits do most of the work: assume breach, least privilege, verify rather than trust, and write it down. One afternoon of practice beats a catalogue of attacks.

Foundation3 min
Why this matters

Skill in security is mostly a set of habits, not a body of facts. The habits are small, boring and repeatable, and they matter more than knowing the name of the latest attack.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • name the four habits that do most of the work
  • apply them to one situation you control today
  • spot the sentence that means a real risk is being ignored

In plain English

People imagine security experts hold a huge catalogue of attacks in their heads. Mostly they hold four habits, and apply them over and over to whatever they are looking at.

That is good news, because habits can be learned in an afternoon and a catalogue cannot. The four below are the ones that keep coming up, in incident write-ups and in post-mortems, over and over.

  • Assume something will get through, and plan for the day it does.
  • Give each person and each program the least access it needs to do its job.
  • Verify rather than trust — check the permission, do not assume the rule is followed.
  • Write it down, because a plan that exists only in someone's memory leaves when they do.

How it works

Each habit is a reaction to a specific, predictable human failure.

  • Assume breach exists because "we would notice" is almost always false — most breaches are found by an outsider, months later.
  • Least privilege exists because access accumulates. Nobody ever asks for less access; they only ask for more.
  • Verify exists because rules drift. The policy says one thing, the actual permissions say another, and only a check finds out which is true.
  • Writing it down exists because knowledge walks out of the door at the same time as the person who had it.

A worked example

A small company keeps one "admin" account for the website, shared by four people, with the password on a note in a drawer. Watch each habit change one thing:

  • Assume breach: if that password leaks, you cannot tell who used it and you cannot tell when — so the fix starts with separate accounts, not with a longer password.
  • Least privilege: the designer does not need admin rights to change a page. Removing that one permission shrinks what a stolen password is worth.
  • Verify: check the account list quarterly. The fifth person on it will be someone who left two years ago.
  • Write it down: one page — who has admin, how to rotate the password, who to call — so recovery does not depend on finding the one person who remembers.

Four habits, one paragraph of work, and the whole situation changed. None of it needed a new product.

The mistake most beginners make

"We are too small to be a target." Automated attacks do not choose targets; they scan everything and take whatever is open. Being small means you are not attacked deliberately, which is a different sentence and a much weaker comfort.

The other mistake is treating security as a project with an end date. It is closer to tidying: the work is small, it is never finished, and the cost of skipping it compounds quietly.

Try it in two minutes

Find one of these and fix only that one, today:

  • An account that more than one person can log into.
  • A password you have used on more than one site.
  • An old account — a job you left, a service you stopped using — that still exists.

Then write one line in your notes about what you changed. That line is the habit starting, and it is worth more than reading another lesson.

Practice / apply

Pick one shared account or one reused password you know about, and fix just that one today. One change that sticks beats a list that does not.

Key takeaways

  • Assume breach, least privilege, verify rather than trust, write it down.
  • Access accumulates quietly; only a check finds out what is actually granted.
  • Automated attacks do not pick targets, so "too small" is not a defence.
  • One change that sticks beats a list that does not.
